claim: Ciona is among the closest living relatives to the vertebrates
source: The tunicate Ciona, which is among the closest living relatives to the vertebrates (Delsuc et al., 2006; Putnam et al., 2008), has emerged as a simple chordate model to characterize multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors and the mechanisms that initiate heart vs. pharyngeal muscle fate choices
evidence: Supported by citations to Delsuc et al., 2006 and Putnam et al., 2008

claim: Ciona has emerged as a simple chordate model to characterize multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors
source: The tunicate Ciona, which is among the closest living relatives to the vertebrates (Delsuc et al., 2006; Putnam et al., 2008), has emerged as a simple chordate model to characterize multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors and the mechanisms that initiate heart vs. pharyngeal muscle fate choices (Kaplan et al., 2015; Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Stolfi et al., 2010; Tolkin and Christiaen, 2016; Wang et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: Ciona tailbud embryos possess two multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors on either side
source: Ciona tailbud embryos possess two multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors on either side.

claim: Cardiopharyngeal progenitors in Ciona emerge from Mesp+ progenitors towards the end of gastrulation
source: Like their vertebrate counterparts, these cells emerge from Mesp+ progenitors towards the end of gastrulation; they are induced by FGF-MAPK signaling and have been termed trunk ventral cells (aka TVCs; [Christiaen et al., 2008; Davidson and Levine, 2003; Davidson et al., 2006; Davidson et al., 2005; Satou et al., 2004; Stolfi et al., 2010])

claim: Cardiopharyngeal progenitors in Ciona are induced by FGF-MAPK signaling
source: Like their vertebrate counterparts, these cells emerge from Mesp+ progenitors towards the end of gastrulation; they are induced by FGF-MAPK signaling and have been termed trunk ventral cells (aka TVCs; [Christiaen et al., 2008; Davidson and Levine, 2003; Davidson et al., 2006; Davidson et al., 2005; Satou et al., 2004; Stolfi et al., 2010])

claim: TVCs activate conserved cardiac markers including Hand, Gata4/5/6 and Nk4/Nkx2-5
source: TVCs activate conserved cardiac markers, including Hand, Gata4/5/6 and Nk4/Nkx2-5, and migrate as polarized pairs of cells, until the left and right pairs meet at the ventral midline and begin to divide asymmetrically along the mediolateral axis (Figure 1A; [Christiaen et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2005; Satou et al., 2004; Stolfi et al., 2010])
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A

claim: TVCs migrate as polarized pairs of cells until they meet at the ventral midline
source: TVCs activate conserved cardiac markers, including Hand, Gata4/5/6 and Nk4/Nkx2-5, and migrate as polarized pairs of cells, until the left and right pairs meet at the ventral midline and begin to divide asymmetrically along the mediolateral axis (Figure 1A; [Christiaen et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2005; Satou et al., 2004; Stolfi et al., 2010])
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A

claim: TVCs divide asymmetrically along the mediolateral axis
source: TVCs activate conserved cardiac markers, including Hand, Gata4/5/6 and Nk4/Nkx2-5, and migrate as polarized pairs of cells, until the left and right pairs meet at the ventral midline and begin to divide asymmetrically along the mediolateral axis (Figure 1A; [Christiaen et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2005; Satou et al., 2004; Stolfi et al., 2010])
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The first oriented asymmetric divisions of TVCs produce small median first heart precursors (FHPs) and large lateral second trunk ventral cells (STVCs)
source: The first oriented asymmetric divisions produce small median first heart precursors (FHPs), and large lateral second trunk ventral cells (STVCs), which specifically activate Tbx1/10 (Davidson et al., 2005; Stolfi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013)

claim: STVCs specifically activate Tbx1/10
source: The first oriented asymmetric divisions produce small median first heart precursors (FHPs), and large lateral second trunk ventral cells (STVCs), which specifically activate Tbx1/10 (Davidson et al., 2005; Stolfi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013)

claim: STVCs divide again to produce small median second heart precursors (SHPs) and large lateral atrial siphon muscle founder cells (ASMFs)
source: STVCs later divide again to produce small median second heart precursors (SHPs), and large lateral atrial siphon muscle founder cells (ASMFs), which activate Ebf (aka COE; [Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Stolfi et al., 2010; Stolfi et al., 2015])

claim: ASMFs activate Ebf
source: STVCs later divide again to produce small median second heart precursors (SHPs), and large lateral atrial siphon muscle founder cells (ASMFs), which activate Ebf (aka COE; [Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Stolfi et al., 2010; Stolfi et al., 2015])

claim: Hand-related (Hand-r) is expressed in the TVCs and maintained in the STVCs and ASMFs after each division
source: The transcription factors Hand-related (Hand-r)/Notrlc, which is expressed in the TVCs and maintained in the STVCs and ASMFs after each division, and Tbx1/10 are required for Ebf activation in the ASMFs

claim: Hand-r and Tbx1/10 are required for Ebf activation in the ASMFs
source: The transcription factors Hand-related (Hand-r)/Notrlc, which is expressed in the TVCs and maintained in the STVCs and ASMFs after each division, and Tbx1/10 are required for Ebf activation in the ASMFs, whereas Nk4/Nkx2.5 represses Tbx1/10 and Ebf expression in the second heart precursors (SHPs)(Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Tolkin and Christiaen, 2016; Wang et al., 2013)

claim: Nk4/Nkx2.5 represses Tbx1/10 and Ebf expression in the second heart precursors (SHPs)
source: The transcription factors Hand-related (Hand-r)/Notrlc, which is expressed in the TVCs and maintained in the STVCs and ASMFs after each division, and Tbx1/10 are required for Ebf activation in the ASMFs, whereas Nk4/Nkx2.5 represses Tbx1/10 and Ebf expression in the second heart precursors (SHPs)(Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Tolkin and Christiaen, 2016; Wang et al., 2013)

claim: Tbx1/10 and Ebf inhibit cardiac markers such as Gata4/5/6 and Hand
source: Conversely, Tbx1/10 and Ebf inhibit cardiac markers, and likely determinants, such as Gata4/5/6 and Hand (Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Stolfi et al., 2010, 2014a; Wang et al., 2013)

claim: dpERK staining was detected in newly born TVCs
source: We detected dpERK staining in the newly born TVCs, marked by the B7.5-lineage-specific Mesp >H2B::mCherry transgene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as previously observed (Davidson et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation

claim: dpERK staining persisted in the TVCs during migration
source: We also detected weaker but persistent dpERK staining in the TVCs during migration (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1)

claim: Following the first and second asymmetric divisions, dpERK staining was successively restricted to the more lateral STVCs and ASMFs
source: Following the first and second asymmetric divisions of the TVCs and STVCs, dpERK staining was successively restricted to the more lateral STVCs and ASMFs, respectively (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)

claim: TVC-specific misexpression of dnFGFR blocked the expression of both Tbx1/10 in the STVCs and Ebf in the ASMFs
source: Consistent with proper TVC induction, Foxf>dnFGFR prevented neither TVC migration nor asymmetric divisions, but it abolished the expression of both Tbx1/10 in the STVCs and Ebf in the ASMFs (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1C showing experimental data

claim: FGF-MAPK signaling is required in the cardiopharyngeal progenitors and/or their progeny for ASM fate specification, beyond the initial TVC induction
source: This data indicate that FGF-MAPK signaling is required in the cardiopharyngeal progenitors and/or their progeny for ASM fate specification, beyond the initial TVC induction
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing dnFGFR effects

claim: Foxf>dnFGFR inhibited Hand-r expression in late TVCs
source: Foxf>dnFGFR inhibited Hand-r expression in late TVCs (Figure 1C), indicating that sustained Hand-r expression requires continuous FGF-MAPK signaling
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1C showing experimental data

claim: Sustained Hand-r expression requires continuous FGF-MAPK signaling
source: Foxf>dnFGFR inhibited Hand-r expression in late TVCs (Figure 1C), indicating that sustained Hand-r expression requires continuous FGF-MAPK signaling

claim: TVC-specific misexpression of M-RasG22V caused both persistent Htr7 expression and ectopic activation of Tbx1/10 in the small median cells following asymmetric divisions
source: Compared to control embryos overexpressing wild-type M-Ras (M-RasWT), TVC-specific gain of M-Ras function caused both persistent Htr7 expression and ectopic activation of Tbx1/10 in the small median cells following asymmetric divisions (Figure 2B,C)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2B,C showing experimental data

claim: Foxf>M-RasG22V-expressing 18hpf larvae displayed ectopic Ebf activation throughout the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm
source: Similarly, Foxf>M-RasG22V-expressing 18hpf larvae displayed ectopic Ebf activation throughout the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm (Figure 2B,C)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2B,C showing experimental data

claim: Forced M-Ras activity is sufficient to upregulate STVC and ASMF markers ectopically
source: These results indicated that forced M-Ras activity is sufficient to upregulate STVC and ASMF markers ectopically

claim: TVC-specific misexpression of MekS220E,S216D caused ectopic expression of Htr7 and Tbx1/10, and Ebf in 15 and 18hpf larvae
source: As seen with M-RasG22V, TVC-specific misexpression of MekS220E,S216D using the Foxf enhancer also caused ectopic expression of Htr7 and Tbx1/10, and Ebf in 15 and 18hpf larvae, respectively (Figure 2B,C)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2B,C showing experimental data

claim: Activity of the canonical FGF-Ras-MEK-ERK pathway is progressively restricted to the STVC and ASMF
source: Taken together, these results indicate that activity of the canonical FGF-Ras-MEK-ERK pathway is progressively restricted to the STVC and ASMF, and is both necessary and sufficient to promote STVC- and ASMF-specific gene expressions

claim: Activity of the canonical FGF-Ras-MEK-ERK pathway is both necessary and sufficient to promote STVC- and ASMF-specific gene expressions
source: Taken together, these results indicate that activity of the canonical FGF-Ras-MEK-ERK pathway is progressively restricted to the STVC and ASMF, and is both necessary and sufficient to promote STVC- and ASMF-specific gene expressions

claim: MEK inhibition during TVC migration (between 9.5 and 12.5 hpf) blocked the expression of Hand-r and Htr7 in late TVCs
source: MEK inhibition during TVC migration (i.e. between 9.5 and 12.5 hpf, Figure 3A) blocked the expression of Hand-r and Htr7 in late TVCs (Figure 3B,E)
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data

claim: U0126 treatments in late TVCs and through the first asymmetric division (between 12 and 15 hpf) blocked both the maintenance of Hand-r and Htr7, and the activation of Tbx1/10 in the STVCs
source: U0126 treatments in late TVCs, and through the first asymmetric division (i.e. between 12 and 15 hpf, Figure 3A) did not alter TVC division patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but it blocked both the maintenance of Hand-r and Htr7, and the activation of Tbx1/10 in the STVCs (Figure 3C,D,F,G)
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data

claim: MEK inhibition in late STVCs and through asymmetric divisions (between 15 and 18 hpf) blocked the ASMF-specific expression of Ebf
source: Finally, MEK inhibition in late STVCs and through asymmetric divisions (i.e. between 15 and 18 hpf) also did not alter STVC divisions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but it blocked the ASMF-specific expression of Ebf (Figure 3H)
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data

claim: Continuous MEK activity is required throughout cardiopharyngeal development to successively activate TVC-, STVC-, and ASMF-expressed genes
source: These results indicate that continuous MEK activity is required throughout cardiopharyngeal development to successively activate TVC-, STVC-, and ASMF-expressed genes

claim: Later MEK inhibition (U0126 incubation between 17 and 20 hpf) did not block the maintenance of Ebf transcription in the ASMPs
source: Using both regular and intron-specific antisense probes, which specifically detect nascent transcripts (Wang et al., 2013), we showed that later MEK inhibition (i.e. U0126 incubation between 17 and 20 hpf) did not block the maintenance of Ebf transcription in the ASMPs (Figure 3I,J)
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data and citation

claim: Sustained MEK activity is required until the onset of Ebf expression, but not beyond
source: This indicates that sustained MEK activity is required until the onset of Ebf expression, but not beyond, and the maintenance of Ebf expression during ASM development is independent of MAPK

claim: The maintenance of Ebf expression during ASM development is independent of MAPK
source: This indicates that sustained MEK activity is required until the onset of Ebf expression, but not beyond, and the maintenance of Ebf expression during ASM development is independent of MAPK

claim: M-RasG22V misexpression caused conspicuous ectopic Ebf expression in the SHPs
source: M-RasG22V misexpression caused conspicuous ectopic Ebf expression in the SHPs, whereas dnFGFR-mediated inhibition of MAPK activity blocked Ebf activation in the lateral ASMFs

claim: dnFGFR-mediated inhibition of MAPK activity blocked Ebf activation in the lateral ASMFs
source: M-RasG22V misexpression caused conspicuous ectopic Ebf expression in the SHPs, whereas dnFGFR-mediated inhibition of MAPK activity blocked Ebf activation in the lateral ASMFs

claim: Localized FGF-MAPK activity is necessary and sufficient for ASMF-specific expression of Ebf
source: These results support the notion that localized FGF-MAPK activity is necessary and sufficient for ASMF-specific expression of Ebf

claim: Hand-r function is necessary for Tbx1/10 activation in the STVCs
source: We validated single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis of Hand-r (Supplementary file 1; [Gandhi et al., 2017]), and determined that Hand-r function is necessary for Tbx1/10 activation in the STVCs (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4A showing experimental data and citation

claim: Co-expression of a CRISPR-resistant Hand-r cDNA (Hand-rPAMmis) rescued Tbx1/10 expression in the STVCs
source: Co-expression of a CRISPR-resistant Hand-r cDNA (Hand-rPAMmis) rescued Tbx1/10 expression in the STVCs, indicating that Tbx1/10 down-regulation in this CRISPR 'background' is specifically due to Hand-r loss-of-function (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4A showing experimental data

claim: Concomitant loss of Hand-r function diminished both endogenous and ectopic Tbx1/10 expression in the STVC and FHP
source: Whereas, misexpression of the constitutively active M-RasG22V caused ectopic Tbx1/10 expression, concomitant loss of Hand-r function diminished both endogenous and ectopic Tbx1/10 expression in the STVC and FHP, respectively (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4A showing experimental data

claim: Hand-r function is necessary for FGF-MAPK-induced activation of Tbx1/10
source: This data indicate that Hand-r function is necessary for FGF-MAPK-induced activation of Tbx1/10

claim: Hand-r over-expression is not sufficient to rescue loss of Tbx1/10 expression due to MAPK inhibition
source: To further probe the epistatic relationships between Hand-r and MAPK signaling upstream of Tbx1/10, we attempted to rescue Tbx1/10 expression in U0126-treated embryos, by over-expressing Hand-r with the TVC-specific Foxf enhancer. Neither did Hand-r over-expression cause ectopic Tbx1/10 activation (in the FHPs), nor was it sufficient to rescue Tbx1/10 expression in 15hpf STVCs (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4B showing experimental data

claim: Both Hand-r and MAPK activities are required to activate Tbx1/10 in the STVCs
source: Taken together, these data indicate that both Hand-r and MAPK activities are required to activate Tbx1/10 in the STVCs

claim: MAPK signaling is restricted to the STVC independently of Hand-r activity
source: These results also imply that MAPK signaling is restricted to the STVC independently of Hand-r activity, which suffice to explain the STVC-specific activation of Tbx1/10

claim: Conserved putative Ets binding sites in the Tbx1/10 enhancer were necessary for reporter gene expression
source: Finally, we isolated a minimal STVC-specific enhancer from the Tbx1/10 locus and identified conserved putative Ets binding sites, which were necessary for reporter gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing experimental data

claim: The FGF-MAPK-Ets pathway directly regulates Tbx1/10 expression in the STVCs
source: This suggests that the FGF-MAPK-Ets pathway directly regulates Tbx1/10 expression in the STVCs
evidence: Inference from experimental data on Ets binding sites

claim: Tbx1/10 function is necessary for Ebf activation
source: We first used previously validated CRIPSR/Cas9 reagents targeting the Tbx1/10 coding region (Tolkin and Christiaen, 2016), to confirm that B7.5-lineage-specific loss of Tbx1/10 function inhibited Ebf activation, and verified that this effect could be rescued by over-expression of a CRISPR/Cas9-resistant Tbx1/10 cDNA, expressed with a minimal TVC-specific Foxf enhancer (Figure 4C; Tbx1/10PAMmis)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4C showing experimental data and citation

claim: Combining CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Tbx1/10 knockout with constitutive MAPK activation using M-RasG22V significantly inhibited both endogenous and ectopic Ebf expression
source: To test whether Tbx1/10 was also required for ectopic Ebf expression in response to MAPK activation (see Figure 2), we combined CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Tbx1/10 knockout with constitutive MAPK activation using the M-RasG22V mutant and observed a significant inhibition of both endogenous and ectopic Ebf expression in the 18hpf ASMF and SHP, respectively (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4C showing experimental data

claim: Tbx1/10 function is necessary for FGF-MAPK-induced expression of Ebf in the ASMFs
source: Taken together, these results show that Tbx1/10 function is necessary for FGF-MAPK-induced expression of Ebf in the ASMFs

claim: Foxf-driven misexpression of Tbx1/10 caused precocious Ebf activation in 15hpf STVCs
source: We realized that Foxf-driven misexpression of Tbx1/10 caused precocious Ebf activation in 15hpf STVCs (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4D,E showing experimental data

claim: Co-expression of Tbx1/10 and M-RasG22V caused both precocious and ectopic Ebf expression in the 15hpf medial and lateral TVC derivatives
source: Indeed, co-expression of Tbx1/10 and M-RasG22V caused both precocious and ectopic Ebf expression in the 15hpf medial and lateral TVC derivatives, which would be FHPs and STVCs in control embryos, respectively

claim: U0126-mediated MEK inhibition from 12 to 15hpf confirmed that MAPK activity is required in parallel to Tbx1/10 for precocious Ebf activation in 15hpf STVCs
source: U0126-mediated MEK inhibition from 12 to 15hpf, that is after the onset of Foxf>Tbx1/10 misexpression, further confirmed that MAPK activity is required in parallel to Tbx1/10 for precocious Ebf activation in 15hpf STVCs (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4D,E showing experimental data

claim: Tbx1/10 and MAPK are both required to activate Ebf in the cell cycle following that of Tbx1/10 onset
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Tbx1/10 and MAPK are both required to activate Ebf in the cell cycle following that of Tbx1/10 onset

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Hand-r mutagenesis strongly inhibited Ebf expression
source: As expected, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Hand-r mutagenesis strongly inhibited Ebf expression, and this effect could be rescued by a CRISPR-resistant Hand-r cDNA (Figure 4F)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4F showing experimental data

claim: Combining loss of Hand-r function with Tbx1/10 misexpression inhibited both the endogenous and ectopic Ebf expression
source: By contrast, combining loss of Hand-r function with Tbx1/10 misexpression inhibited both the endogenous and ectopic Ebf expression (Figure 4F), indicating that Hand-r is also required in parallel to Tbx1/10 for Ebf activation in the ASMFs
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4F showing experimental data

claim: Hand-r is required in parallel to Tbx1/10 for Ebf activation in the ASMFs
source: By contrast, combining loss of Hand-r function with Tbx1/10 misexpression inhibited both the endogenous and ectopic Ebf expression (Figure 4F), indicating that Hand-r is also required in parallel to Tbx1/10 for Ebf activation in the ASMFs

claim: Coherent feed-forward circuits govern the sequential activation of Hand-r, Tbx1/10 and Ebf in response to continuous but progressively restricted FGF-MAPK inputs
source: Taken together, these analyses suggest that coherent feed-forward circuits govern the sequential activation of Hand-r, Tbx1/10 and Ebf in response to continuous but progressively restricted FGF-MAPK inputs (Figure 4G)
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results, supported by Figure 4G

claim: Treatments with cytochalasin B starting before TVC divisions (12 hpf) did not block Tbx1/10 or Ebf expression in embryos fixed after their normal onset
source: Treatments starting before TVC divisions (12 hpf) did not block Tbx1/10 or Ebf expression in embryos fixed after their normal onset at either 16 or 19hpf, respectively (Figure 5B,C)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5B,C showing experimental data

claim: Cytochalasin B treatment starting between the first and second asymmetric divisions (15hpf) did not block localized Ebf expression at 19hpf
source: Similarly, treatment starting between the first and second asymmetric divisions (15hpf) did not block localized Ebf expression at 19hpf (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5C showing experimental data

claim: Tbx1/10 and Ebf activations occur by default in the absence of cytokinesis
source: This indicates that Tbx1/10 and Ebf activations occur by default in the absence of cytokinesis, most likely because FGF-MAPK signaling persists throughout the shared cytoplasm

claim: Misexpression of Cdkn1b.a, Cdkn1b.b, and Wee1 using the TVC-specific Foxf enhancer efficiently inhibited TVC divisions
source: We used the TVC-specific Foxf enhancer to misexpress these negative regulators of cell cycle progression, monitored cell divisions and assayed Tbx1/10 expression at 15hpf, when control TVCs have divided and the lateral-most STVCs normally express Tbx1/10. Each perturbation efficiently inhibited TVC divisions, such that only two cells were visible on either side of the embryos (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5D showing experimental data

claim: In delayed TVCs, Tbx1/10 expression was strongly reduced compared to control STVCs
source: In these delayed TVCs, Tbx1/10 expression was strongly reduced compared to control STVCs (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5D showing experimental data

claim: 20% to 40% of the delayed TVCs expressed Tbx1/10 to variable extents
source: However, 20% to 40% of the delayed TVCs expressed Tbx1/10 to variable extents

claim: The cardiopharyngeal regulatory network can qualitatively unfold independently of cell cycle progression, but the latter is necessary for Tbx1/10 expression to its wild-type levels
source: This suggests that the cardiopharyngeal regulatory network can qualitatively unfold independently of cell cycle progression, but the latter is necessary for Tbx1/10 expression to its wild-type levels

claim: Wee1 misexpression strongly delays cell cycle progression, blocking cell divisions in a substantial fraction of embryos
source: First, we scored the proportions of embryos with delayed STVCs or conspicuous ASMFs at each time point and showed that Wee1 misexpression strongly delays cell cycle progression, blocking cell divisions in a substantial fraction of embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing experimental data

claim: Ebf can turn on in arrested STVCs that failed to divide upon Wee1 misexpression
source: Analyses of 18hpf larvae, fixed approximately 2 hr after the documented onset of Ebf expression in ASMFs (Razy-Krajka et al., 2014), indicated that Ebf can turn on in arrested STVCs that failed to divide upon Wee1 misexpression (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5E showing experimental data and citation

claim: Wee1-induced mitosis inhibition delays Ebf accumulation
source: These semi-quantitative analyses suggest that the cardiopharyngeal network can eventually unfold independently of cell divisions, leading to high levels of Ebf expression, albeit with a delay. This suggests that STVC division entrains Ebf upregulation in early ASMFs

claim: STVC division entrains Ebf upregulation in early ASMFs
source: These semi-quantitative analyses suggest that the cardiopharyngeal network can eventually unfold independently of cell divisions, leading to high levels of Ebf expression, albeit with a delay. This suggests that STVC division entrains Ebf upregulation in early ASMFs

claim: Delayed STVCs failed to activate the pan-cardiac Lrp4/8, and the SHP-markers Kirr and Dach
source: Indeed, delayed STVCs failed to activate the pan-cardiac Lrp4/8, and the SHP-markers Kirr and Dach (Figure 5F; [Wang et al., 2017])
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5F showing experimental data and citation

claim: Coupling STVC division with localized FGF-MAPK activity and timed Ebf upregulation permits the localized activation of Ebf and the emergence of cardiac progenitors
source: This indicated that coupling STVC division with localized FGF-MAPK activity and timed Ebf upregulation permits the localized activation of Ebf and the emergence of cardiac progenitors

claim: Ebf transcription gradually lost its sensitivity to MAPK inhibition between 16 and 17hpf
source: This analysis revealed that Ebf transcription gradually lost its sensitivity to MAPK inhibition between 16 and 17hpf, that is during the first hour of the ASMF cycle when Ebf mRNAs normally accumulate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B showing experimental data

claim: Ebf misexpression caused precocious and ectopic activation of the endogenous locus in the STVCs, and in the MAPK-negative SHPs
source: Assaying endogenous Ebf transcription with intronic probes demonstrated that, in addition to its normal expression in the ASMFs, Ebf misexpression caused precocious and ectopic activation of the endogenous locus in the STVCs, and in the MAPK-negative SHPs, respectively (Figure 6C–F)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6C–F showing experimental data

claim: Ebf transcription bypasses both requirements for cell-division coupling and MAPK inputs if high levels of Ebf gene products are present in the cell
source: This result suggests that Ebf transcription bypasses both requirements for cell-division coupling and MAPK inputs if high levels of Ebf gene products are present in the cell

claim: Transcription of the endogenous Ebf locus became independent of early MAPK activity upon misexpression of an Ebf cDNA
source: We observed that transcription of the endogenous Ebf locus became independent of early MAPK activity upon misexpression of an Ebf cDNA, further supporting the notion that high levels of Ebf expression suffice to maintain Ebf transcription independently of MAPK activity

claim: High levels of Ebf expression suffice to maintain Ebf transcription independently of MAPK activity
source: We observed that transcription of the endogenous Ebf locus became independent of early MAPK activity upon misexpression of an Ebf cDNA, further supporting the notion that high levels of Ebf expression suffice to maintain Ebf transcription independently of MAPK activity

claim: Although Ebf can be activated precociously in a MAPK-dependent manner, its expression shuts off in the SHPs upon MAPK inhibition following STVC division
source: This suggests that, although Ebf can be activated precociously in a MAPK-dependent manner, its expression shuts off in the SHPs upon MAPK inhibition following STVC division

claim: Delaying STVC divisions extends the period of MAPK-dependent Ebf transcription
source: We reasoned that, if cell divisions entrain Ebf accumulation and the transition to a MAPK-independent autoregulative mode, then delaying STVC divisions should extend the period of MAPK-dependent Ebf transcription. We tested this possibility by expressing Wee1 under the control of the STVC-specific T6 enhancer, and treated embryos with U0126 at 17hpf, which inhibited the maintenance of Ebf transcription in only 15% to 20% of the control embryos (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). The proportion of embryos showing U0126-sensitive Ebf transcription increased to almost 50% upon Tbx1/10>Wee1 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data

claim: Inhibiting the G2/M transition delays the accumulation of Ebf gene products, thus postponing the transition from a low level/MAPK-dependent to an high level/MAPK-independent and self-activating mode of Ebf regulation
source: which is consistent with our hypothesis that inhibiting the G2/M transition delays the accumulation of Ebf gene products, thus postponing the transition from a low level/MAPK-dependent to an high level/MAPK-independent and self-activating mode of Ebf regulation

claim: Hand-r, Tbx1/10, ongoing MAPK signaling and cell-cycle-regulated transcriptional input(s) govern the onset and initial accumulation of Ebf gene products during the first hour of the ASMF cycle
source: We propose a model for Ebf regulation whereby Hand-r, Tbx1/10, ongoing MAPK signaling and cell-cycle-regulated transcriptional input(s) govern the onset and initial accumulation of Ebf gene products during the first hour of the ASMF cycle, whereas the maintenance of Ebf expression relies primarily on MAPK-independent autoactivation, following initial accumulation (Figure 7)
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental data, supported by Figure 7

claim: The maintenance of Ebf expression relies primarily on MAPK-independent autoactivation, following initial accumulation
source: We propose a model for Ebf regulation whereby Hand-r, Tbx1/10, ongoing MAPK signaling and cell-cycle-regulated transcriptional input(s) govern the onset and initial accumulation of Ebf gene products during the first hour of the ASMF cycle, whereas the maintenance of Ebf expression relies primarily on MAPK-independent autoactivation, following initial accumulation (Figure 7)
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental data, supported by Figure 7

claim: The progressive restriction of FGF-MAPK signaling follows oriented and asymmetric cell divisions of multipotent progenitors and patterns the ascidian cardiopharyngeal mesoderm in space and time
source: Here, we demonstrated that the progressive restriction of FGF-MAPK signaling follows oriented and asymmetric cell divisions of multipotent progenitors and patterns the ascidian cardiopharyngeal mesoderm in space and time

claim: Dynamic FGF-MAPK activity patterns lead to the localized expression of Hand-r, Tbx1/10 and Ebf in fate-restricted pharyngeal muscle precursors
source: Dynamic FGF-MAPK activity patterns lead to the localized expression of Hand-r, Tbx1/10 and Ebf in fate-restricted pharyngeal muscle precursors, and their concomitant exclusion for first and second heart precursors

claim: Coherent feedforward circuits encode the successive activations of Hand-r, Tbx1/10 and Ebf
source: We show that coherent feedforward circuits encode the successive activations of Hand-r, Tbx1/10 and Ebf, whereas cell divisions entrain the progression of this regulatory sequence and thus define the timing of gene expression

claim: Cell divisions entrain the progression of the regulatory sequence and thus define the timing of gene expression
source: We show that coherent feedforward circuits encode the successive activations of Hand-r, Tbx1/10 and Ebf, whereas cell divisions entrain the progression of this regulatory sequence and thus define the timing of gene expression

claim: The initiation of Ebf expression depends on MAPK activity in early ASMF, until Ebf accumulation permits MAPK-independent auto-activation
source: Finally, we provide evidence that the initiation of Ebf expression depends on MAPK activity in early ASMF, until Ebf accumulation permits MAPK-independent auto-activation

claim: The switch from MAPK-dependent to MAPK-independent Ebf expression corresponds to the transition from a cardiopharyngeal multipotent state to a committed pharyngeal muscle identity
source: Given the potent anti-cardiogenic, and pro-pharyngeal muscle effects of Ebf (Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Stolfi et al., 2010), we surmise that the latter switch corresponds to the transition from a cardiopharyngeal multipotent state to a committed pharyngeal muscle identity
evidence: Inference from experimental data and cited literature

claim: MAPK signaling is maintained only in the lateral-most daughter cells following each asymmetric division of multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors
source: Our results demonstrate that MAPK signaling is maintained only in the lateral-most daughter cells following each asymmetric division of multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors - the TVCs and STVCs

claim: Asymmetric maintenance of MAPK signaling is necessary and sufficient for the progressive and localized deployment of the pharyngeal muscle network
source: This asymmetric maintenance is necessary and sufficient for the progressive and localized deployment of the pharyngeal muscle network

claim: During TVC induction, asymmetrical maintenance of sustained FGF-MAPK signaling involves intrinsic Cdc42-dependent polarity of the founder cells
source: At this stage, asymmetrical maintenance of sustained FGF-MAPK signaling involves intrinsic Cdc42-dependent polarity of the founder cells, which promotes polarized cell-matrix adhesion of the prospective TVC membrane to the ventral epidermis

claim: Differential integrin-mediated adhesion promotes localized MAPK activation, leading to TVC induction
source: The latter differential integrin-mediated adhesion promotes localized MAPK activation, leading to TVC induction (Cooley et al., 2011; Norton et al., 2013)

claim: Adhesion- and caveolin-dependent polarized FGFR recycling during mitosis accounts for the localized activation of MAPK in the prospective TVCs
source: It has been proposed that adhesion- and caveolin-dependent polarized FGFR recycling during mitosis accounts for the localized activation of MAPK in the prospective TVCs (Cota and Davidson, 2015)

claim: Constitutively active forms of M-Ras and Mek1/2 were sufficient to bypass the loss of MAPK activity, and impose pharyngeal muscle specification
source: However, the fact that constitutively active forms of M-Ras and Mek1/2 were sufficient to bypass the loss of MAPK activity, and impose pharyngeal muscle specification, indicates that differential FGF-MAPK activity is regulated upstream of M-Ras

claim: Differential FGF-MAPK activity is regulated upstream of M-Ras
source: However, the fact that constitutively active forms of M-Ras and Mek1/2 were sufficient to bypass the loss of MAPK activity, and impose pharyngeal muscle specification, indicates that differential FGF-MAPK activity is regulated upstream of M-Ras

claim: Perturbations of the FGF-Ras-MEK pathway can alter cardiopharyngeal cell division patterns
source: Our preliminary analyses indicate that perturbations of the FGF-Ras-MEK pathway can alter cardiopharyngeal cell division patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing experimental data

claim: Whole genome analyses indicate that heart-specific de novo gene expression requires MAPK inhibition
source: As shown in our companion paper (Wang et al., 2017), whole genome analyses indicate that heart-specific de novo gene expression requires MAPK inhibition (Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to companion paper

claim: Nk4/Nkx2-5-mediated repression in other species involves the co-repressor Groucho/TLE
source: for instance, Nk4/Nkx2.5-mediated repression in other species involves the co-repressor Groucho/TLE (Choi et al., 1999), which is strongly expressed in the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm (Razy-Krajka et al., 2014)

claim: In flies, MAPK-mediated phosphorylation of Groucho inhibits its repressor function
source: and, in flies, MAPK-mediated phosphorylation of Groucho inhibits its repressor function (Cinnamon et al., 2008; Cinnamon and Paroush, 2008; Hasson et al., 2005)

claim: Persistent MAPK signaling may dampen Groucho/TLE-mediated repressive inputs on cell-specific regulatory genes like Ebf
source: Therefore, it is possible that persistent MAPK signaling dampens Groucho/TLE-mediated repressive inputs on cell-specific regulatory genes like Ebf
evidence: Speculation based on knowledge from other systems

claim: Experimental misexpression of Ebf throughout the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm suffice to inhibit heart development
source: Experimental misexpression of Ebf throughout the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm suffice to inhibit heart development (Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Stolfi et al., 2010)

claim: Multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors express Ets1/2 and Elk
source: However, multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors express Ets1/2 and Elk, two common transcriptional effectors of FGF/MAPK signaling in Ciona (Bertrand et al., 2003; Christiaen et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2006; Gainous et al., 2015)

claim: Ets1/2 has been implicated in the initial FGF-MAPK-dependent induction of multipotent TVCs
source: Ets1/2 has been implicated in the initial FGF-MAPK-dependent induction of multipotent TVCs (Christiaen et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2006)

claim: Ets1/2 expression is progressively restricted to the lateral-most progenitors following each division
source: and its expression is also progressively restricted to the lateral-most progenitors following each division (Razy-Krajka et al., 2014)

claim: Ebf expression is maintained for several days in the ASMF derivatives as they differentiate into body wall and siphon muscles
source: Since Ebf expression is maintained for several days in the ASMF derivatives as they differentiate into body wall and siphon muscles (Razy-Krajka et al., 2014)

claim: The G1 phase has been shown to be particularly conducive to the expression of fate-specific regulators in mammalian pluripotent stem cells
source: Although the mechanisms remain elusive, it is likely that this requires the M/G1 transition, as the G1 phase has been shown to be particularly conducive to the expression of fate-specific regulators in mammalian pluripotent stem cells (Dalton, 2015; Pauklin et al., 2016; Pauklin and Vallier, 2013; Soufi and Dalton, 2016)

claim: Early FGF-MAPK inputs induce and maintain multipotent cardiopharyngeal states in Ciona
source: We now know that these early FGF-MAPK inputs induce and maintain multipotent cardiopharyngeal states in Ciona, including the Tbx1/10+ multipotent progenitors that eventually produce the second heart lineage ([Razy-Krajka et al., 2014; Stolfi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013], [Wang et al., 2017] and this study)
evidence: Supported by citations and current study

claim: In vertebrates, regulatory interplay between Fgf8 and Fgf10 signaling and Tbx1 is required for development of both pharyngeal arch and second heart field derivatives
source: Similarly, in vertebrates, regulatory interplay between Fgf8 and Fgf10 signaling and Tbx1 is required for development of both pharyngeal arch and second heart field derivatives, presumably in part by maintaining an undifferentiated and proliferative state (Abu-Issa et al., 2002; Aggarwal et al., 2006; Brown et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2004; Ilagan et al., 2006; Kelly and Papaioannou, 2007; Park et al., 2006; Park et al., 2008; Vitelli et al., 2002b; Watanabe et al., 2010; Watanabe et al., 2012)

claim: In fish, FGF signaling is necessary for cardiomyocyte addition at the arterial pole
source: In fish, FGF signaling is necessary for cardiomyocyte addition at the arterial pole, in a manner reminiscent of its role in second heart field development (de Pater et al., 2009; Lazic and Scott, 2011)

claim: FGF signaling acts in successive phases, and its inhibition is necessary for final myocardial specification and differentiation
source: Notably, FGF signaling acts in successive phases, and its inhibition is necessary for final myocardial specification and differentiation (Hutson et al., 2010; Marques et al., 2008; Tirosh-Finkel et al., 2010; van Wijk et al., 2009)

claim: Continued FGF signaling beyond the multipotent mesodermal progenitor stages was shown to promote smooth muscle and epicardial differential in the heart
source: Conversely, continued FGF signaling beyond the multipotent mesodermal progenitor stages was shown to promote smooth muscle and epicardial differential in the heart (Hutson et al., 2010; van Wijk et al., 2009)

claim: Continued FGF signaling promotes myoblast specification and/or skeletal muscle differentiation in the head
source: and also myoblast specification and/or skeletal muscle differentiation in the head, with the expression of FGF ligands being maintained in the pharyngeal arches (Bothe et al., 2011; Buckingham and Vincent, 2009; Michailovici et al., 2015; Michailovici et al., 2014; von Scheven et al., 2006)

claim: FGF-MAPK signaling plays evolutionary conserved roles during chordate cardiopharyngeal development
source: Taken together, these and our data suggest that FGF-MAPK signaling plays evolutionary conserved roles during chordate cardiopharyngeal development, by promoting the specification of successive mesodermal and Tbx1+ multipotent states, and a fate-restricted non-cardiac muscle identity, while MAPK inhibition is required for myocardial specification and differentiation in the first and second heart field, successively
evidence: Inference from current study and cited literature
